---
title: "Worked example — editing a LaTeX paper"
subtitle: "Bibliography cleanup, table reformatting, and a careful section rewrite, with Claude Code in the driver's seat."
---

This walks through using Claude Code on a paper draft. The tasks are
intentionally pedestrian — they're the kind of thing you'd otherwise hand
to an RA, except the loop here is minutes instead of days.

::: {.callout-note}
The prompts below are verbatim — you can copy them. Replace file names
with yours.
:::

## Setup

```bash
cd ~/Desktop/papers/wage-paper
claude
```

Before doing anything, give Claude an orientation pass:

> "Read the project. Tell me what's here, what `paper.tex` is about in one
> paragraph, and which auxiliary files (.bib, tables, figures) it depends
> on."

This takes 30 seconds. The benefit is that subsequent prompts can refer to
"the main paper" or "the auxiliary files" without you re-explaining each
time.

## Task 1 — bibliography cleanup

Bibtex files rot. Entries get added during a co-author binge and never
cleaned up; some are cited, some aren't, some have subtly wrong years.

> "Look at every `\cite`, `\citet`, and `\citep` in `paper.tex` and
> appendix.tex. List entries in `references.bib` that are **never** cited.
> Don't delete anything — just give me the list."

You'll get something like:

```
Unused entries (12 of 87):
  - smith2003
  - jones1999  (note: cited as `jones99` elsewhere — possible typo)
  - ...
```

The flag on `jones1999` is a real win: it's the kind of thing you'd miss
on a manual pass. Now:

> "Remove the unused entries from `references.bib`. For `jones1999`, fix
> the citation key inconsistency: replace `\cite{jones99}` with
> `\cite{jones1999}` everywhere, and keep the `jones1999` entry."

Read the diff before approving. Compile. Done.

## Task 2 — table reformatting

You inherit a paper from a co-author and the tables are a mix of
hand-written `tabular` environments, `booktabs`, and one orphaned
`longtable`. You want everything on `booktabs` with a consistent style.

> "Show me the source of each `table` environment in `paper.tex` and the
> standalone .tex files in `tables/`. Identify which use `\toprule`,
> `\midrule`, `\bottomrule` (booktabs) and which still use `\hline`. Don't
> change anything yet."

Once you see the inventory:

> "Convert all `\hline`-based tables to booktabs style: `\toprule` at the
> top, `\midrule` between header and body and around any subgroup, and
> `\bottomrule` at the end. Keep column alignments and content untouched.
> Make sure `\usepackage{booktabs}` is in `paper.tex`."

::: {.callout-warning}
Here is where you must read the diffs carefully. Table edits are the
classic place where an LLM "tidies up" content you didn't ask it to tidy
— a stray digit gets reformatted, a column header gets rephrased. Read
every diff and reject anything that touches the *content* rather than the
*formatting*.
:::

## Task 3 — a careful section rewrite

This is the one where you should slow down. Claude can rewrite prose
beautifully and confidently, including arguments you don't actually make.
Treat this as **collaborative editing**, not delegation.

> "Read section 3 (Empirical Strategy) of `paper.tex`. Don't change
> anything yet. Tell me: (a) what the central identification claim is in
> your reading; (b) any place where the text references something that's
> not in the data section or the appendix; (c) any sentences that are
> longer than 35 words or have more than two subordinate clauses."

That's an audit, not a rewrite. Read what it says.

If you agree with the audit:

> "Rewrite only the sentences you flagged in (c) for length. Preserve every
> claim. Do not introduce new arguments. Do not change any numbers or
> citations. Show me the diff sentence by sentence."

Approve, reject, or tweak each sentence individually. You stay the author.

## Task 4 — compile and check

> "Run `latexmk -pdf paper.tex` and tell me if there are any errors,
> warnings, or unresolved citations."

Claude runs the build, parses the log, and tells you what's broken. If a
table now has a misaligned column, you'll find out before you re-read the
PDF.

## What this saved you

- **Bibliography cleanup:** ~2 hours of grunt work compressed to ~10
  minutes of supervision.
- **Table reformatting:** would have taken half a day; now ~15 minutes.
- **Section audit:** the slowest task, but most valuable — Claude is
  willing to flag long sentences your eye no longer sees.

## What it did not do

- It did not decide what your contribution is.
- It did not check whether your identification strategy is credible — it
  read what you wrote and described it back to you.
- It did not fact-check your citations against the cited papers.

These remain your job.

## Common traps in this workflow

::: {.callout-warning}
**Don't let it "improve" prose you didn't ask it to.** Tell it explicitly
what to change and what to leave alone. "Don't introduce new arguments"
is a sentence worth typing every single time.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
**Don't trust new citations it adds.** If it adds a `\cite{...}` for a
paper you didn't tell it about, treat that as a hallucinated citation
until you've personally confirmed the entry exists in your `.bib` and
the cited claim matches the source. See
[Hallucinations](../pitfalls/hallucinations.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Use plan mode for multi-file edits.** Hit `Shift+Tab` until you see
"plan mode", then ask. Claude will write a plan ("I'll change these 4
files, here's what each change does"), wait for your approval, and only
then edit.
:::
